title: A Siege Acted Out in Clay
overview: God tells Ezekiel, living among the exiles in Babylon, to act out the coming siege of Jerusalem with a clay model, long months lying on his side, and starvation rations.

parts.label: A model city under attack (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Ezekiel draws Jerusalem on a clay brick and surrounds it with a miniature siege: lookout towers, an earth ramp, army camps and battering rams. The iron cooking plate set between him and the city likely pictures a siege no one can break, or a wall between God and the city, though its exact meaning is debated.

parts.label: Lying on each side (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: He lies on his left side for 390 days for the northern kingdom of Israel, then on his right for 40 days for the southern kingdom of Judah, a day for each year of their wrongdoing. What those numbers count is uncertain, and Christians have also read his carrying the people's guilt as a picture of Jesus bearing the sins of others.

parts.label: Starvation rations (vv. 9-11)
parts.note: He must make bread from a mix of whatever grains and beans can be scraped together, the coarse food of the very poor. Each day he gets roughly eight ounces of food and about half a liter of water, showing how little people would have during the siege.

parts.label: Bread baked over dung (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Baking over human waste would make the food ritually impure under Israel's law, picturing exiles forced to eat food their law forbade in foreign lands. Ezekiel, a priest who had kept the food laws all his life, protests, and God allows cow dung instead, a common fuel in that region.

parts.label: What the signs mean (vv. 16-17)
parts.note: God spells it out: Jerusalem's food supply, the bread that life depends on, will be cut off. People will measure out food and water in fear and stare at one another in shock as they waste away.

disagreement: Readers differ on what the 390 and 40 days actually stand for, and on whether Ezekiel physically performed all this in public or is describing something he saw in a vision.
think: When has seeing something acted out or shown to you reached you in a way that words alone did not?
